newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: SKorea to boost competitivenss by lifting tariffs.
newsitem.headline: SKorea to boost competitivenss by lifting tariffs.

text.p: South Korea will remove import tariffs on 10 raw materials from next month as a part of the government's drive to enhance corporate competitiveness, the Ministry of Finance and Economy said on Thursday.
The tariffs are currently set between one to two percent.
"This step will help companies to improve competitiveness and boost exports by saving part of high production costs," a Finance Ministry official told Reuters.

The 10 items are ores and concentrates for eight metallic items -- copper, lead, zinc, aluminium, zirconium, molybdenum, manganese and chrome -- and ferrous waste/scrap and wool. South Korea depends entirely on imports for these items, he said.
In calendar 1995, South Korea's imports of these 10 items totalled $2.2 billion.
The ministry has not decided on exact date for the tax removal.
The government has been taking steps to reduce next year's current account deficit through thrift, saving efforts and improvement of competitiveness.
Earlier this month, South Korean President Kim Young-sam told his Cabinet to try to reduce the nation's current account deficit for calendar 1997 to half this year's level.
South Korea's current account deficit was expected to more than double to about $20 billion this year, compared with a shortfall of $8.9 billion in 1995.
The government has put its top policy priority on enhancing corporate competitiveness, which has been suffering from high production costs and low management efficiency.
The official said the government expects the removal of tariffs to reduce the country's producer price index growth by 0.3 of a basis point.
South Korea's producer price index rose 3.3 percent in October on the year, up from a 2.3 percent in September and down from a 3.9 percent a year earlier.
In June, import tariffs were also removed on six other raw materials -- bituminous coal, lumber, iron ore, cotton, rubber and pig iron.
